input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-603: Computational Problem Solving. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on the application of computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics include: expression of algorithms in pseudo-code and a programming language; elementary data structures such as lists, trees and graphs; problem solving using recursion; and debugging and testing. Assignments (both in class and homework) requiring a pseudo-code solution and implementation in a programming language are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[llvm-language-reference]
LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow. A module contains global values, functions, declarations, and metadata. A function contains basic blocks, and every basic block ends with a terminator instruction. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Load and store instructions make memory access explicit. Valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules. The verifier reports IR that violates those rules. Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

[rit-csci-603]
This course focuses on the application of computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics include: expression of algorithms in pseudo-code and a programming language; elementary data structures such as lists, trees and graphs; problem solving using recursion; and debugging and testing. Assignments (both in class and homework) requiring a pseudo-code solution and implementation in a programming language are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: Computational thinking relies on abstraction, decomposition, and algorithmic expression to transform complex problems into manageable computational steps.
beats.example: A student breaks down a sorting problem into identifying the input list, comparing elements, and arranging them in order before writing pseudo-code.
beats.title: Foundations of Computational Thinking
beats.visualDirection: Display a split screen: left side shows a messy real-world problem, right side shows a clean pseudo-code block with labeled abstraction and decomposition steps.

beats.claim: Algorithms must be expressed in pseudo-code first, then translated into a concrete programming language to ensure clarity and correctness before execution.
beats.example: A pseudo-code function for finding the maximum value in a list is converted to Python, preserving the logical flow while adding syntax and type constraints.
beats.title: Pseudo-Code and Language Expression
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of the pseudo-code and Python implementation, highlighting how each pseudo-code line maps to a specific Python statement.

beats.claim: Lists serve as a fundamental data structure for storing ordered collections of elements, enabling sequential access and manipulation in algorithms.
beats.example: A student uses a Python list to store test scores, then iterates through it to calculate the average using a simple loop.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Lists
beats.visualDirection: Animate a list growing with each new score added, then show a pointer moving through the list to demonstrate sequential access during iteration.

beats.claim: Trees provide a hierarchical data structure that organizes elements into parent-child relationships, optimizing search and traversal operations.
beats.example: A binary tree represents a file system where directories are nodes and files are leaf nodes, allowing efficient path resolution.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Trees
beats.visualDirection: Render a binary tree diagram with labeled parent-child links, highlighting how a search path branches down to a target leaf node.

beats.claim: Graphs model relationships between entities using nodes and edges, enabling the representation of networks, routes, and dependencies.
beats.example: A student models a city's road network as a graph where intersections are nodes and roads are edges to find the shortest path.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Graphs
beats.visualDirection: Draw a simple graph with labeled nodes and directed edges, then trace a path from a start node to an end node using a step-by-step animation.

beats.claim: Recursion solves problems by breaking them into smaller, self-similar subproblems, each solved by calling the function itself until a base case is reached.
beats.example: A factorial function calculates n! by multiplying n with the result of factorial(n-1), stopping when n equals 1.
beats.title: Recursive Problem Solving
beats.visualDirection: Show a recursive call stack expanding downward with each function call, then collapsing upward as base cases return values.

beats.claim: Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while systematic testing verifies that program behavior matches expected contracts and state transitions.
beats.example: A student uses print statements and a test harness to verify that a sorting algorithm correctly handles edge cases like empty lists or single-element lists.
beats.title: Debugging and Testing Protocols
beats.visualDirection: Display a debugger interface highlighting a runtime error, then show a test suite passing/failing based on input/output contracts.

beats.claim: Programs must be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, and contracts to ensure predictable and verifiable behavior.
beats.example: A student defines a class with explicit attributes and methods, ensuring that each method updates state according to a documented contract.
beats.title: State and Control Flow Management
beats.visualDirection: Show a state machine diagram transitioning between states, with arrows labeled by method calls and state updates.

beats.claim: Every factual claim, example, and visual direction must cite supplied source IDs and reuse technical terms from those sources to enable local verification and deterministic local
beats.example: A student cross-references the pseudo-code implementation with the source excerpts, ensuring that terms like 'basic blocks', 'terminator instruction', and 'namespace' are correctly applied.
beats.title: Verification and Local Expander Preparation
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist overlay with checkboxes for each source ID, technical term reuse, and claim verification, ready for the local expander to generate full narration.

beats.claim: The practical analysis checklist ensures that all course objectives are met by verifying abstraction, data structure usage, recursion, debugging, and testing protocols in the final
beats.example: A student reviews their assignment against the checklist, confirming that pseudo-code and code match, data structures are correctly implemented, recursion is applied, and tests pass.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a clean, printable checklist with sections for each beat, checkboxes for claim verification, and space for instructor notes.

learningObjectives: 1. Define and apply the core components of computational thinking: abstraction, decomposition, and algorithmic expression in pseudo-code and a target
2. Demonstrate the construction and manipulation of elementary data structures (lists, trees, graphs) to model problem domains accurately.
3. Execute recursive problem-solving strategies and implement systematic debugging and testing protocols to verify program correctness.
